query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, optimized amount of boron during alloy processing will cause boron segregation to the internal lamellar boundaries of eutectic high‐entropy alloys, thereby reinforcing these interfaces to both inhibit microcrack initiation and impede dislocation motion. This should result in simultaneous improvements in tensile strength and room-temperature ductility relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys featuring dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that are prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled trace addition of boron into the alloy composition during processing (e.g., during casting/heat-treatment) to promote selective segregation at internal boundaries.
generation.conditions: Process the alloys under conventional casting and annealing conditions that permit boron segregation without forming excessive secondary phases; test under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The internal lamellar colony boundaries, where boron is expected to segregate and lower interfacial energy.
generation.mechanism: Boron atoms preferentially segregate to the internal boundaries, thereby enhancing interfacial cohesion and reducing stress concentration sites that would otherwise nucleate microcracks. Concurrently, the strengthened interfaces help impede dislocation motion in a manner analogous to grain-boundary strengthening, boosting tensile strength without sacrificing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar colony alloy, the boron-doped alloy should display a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and ductility (as evidenced by higher fracture strains), with delayed onset and reduced density of microcracks during tensile deformation.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloys processed without boron doping, which typically exhibit high strength accompanied by limited ductility and brittle failure initiated at internal lamellar boundaries.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only when boron is added within an optimal concentration range that allows for effective interface segregation. Exceeding the solubility limit or inappropriate processing conditions could lead to the formation of unwanted brittle phases or insufficient interfacial modification.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvements are supported by the known benefits of boundary doping in similar systems, the precise quantitative gains in strength and ductility remain uncertain and will depend on the exact dopant level and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples with identical processing conditions: one set of eutectic high-entropy alloys with a trace addition of boron (within the optimized range) and a control set without boron. Utilize identical melting, casting, and heat-treatment protocols. Afterwards, conduct a series of room-temperature tensile tests alongside microstructural evaluations (using transmission electron microscopy and atom probe tomography) to assess boundary chemistry and microcrack formation.
measurements: Density and distribution of microcracks from microscopy
Evidence of boron segregation at lamellar boundaries (via APT or EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples fail to show both statistically significant improvements in tensile strength and ductility compared to the control; or if microstructural analysis does not confirm effective boron segregation at the internal boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.
